[front matter] ADVERTISEMENT.
[front matter] One of the Parker Society’s objects, as stated in the
[front matter] first of its Laws, is “the printing, as may appear desirable,
[front matter] of some of the Early English translations of the Foreign
[front matter] Reformers.” Accordingly, the re-publishing of the English
[front matter] Version of the Decades of Bullinger was announced, as in
[front matter] the contemplation of the Council of the Society, in a List
[front matter] which was appended to the Second Annual Report; and the
[front matter] first volume is now, at length, presented to the subscribers.
[front matter] The edition, which is here reprinted, is that of 1587, which
[front matter] scarcely differs at all, in any material respects, from the
[front matter] former edition of 1584, and very little from that of 1577;
[front matter] but any important variations between the translation and the
[front matter] original Latin are carefully specified in the notes. The Ver-
[front matter] sion was made, as stated in the title-page, “by H.I. Student
[front matter] in Divinitie,’—‘“ a person,” according to Strype’s testimony,
[front matter] “of eminency in the Church!.”
[front matter] These Decades, it is conceived, possess a peculiar claim
[front matter] on the regard of the members of the Church of England.
[front matter] For not only was Bullinger “ well-deserving of this nation for
[front matter] his kind entertainment and harbour of our divines and _ scho-
[front matter] lars that fled abroad in Queen Mary’s reign, and of note
[front matter] for that friendship and correspondence ever after maintained
[front matter] between him and them?;” but several of his writings, as they
[front matter] became known here, were eminently appreciated by our theo-
[front matter] logians and religious persons of the era of the Reformation’.
[front matter] 1 Strype, Ann. book π΄ chap. 10, p. 145, Vol. πι. part 2. ed. Oxf.
[front matter] 1824.
[front matter] 2 Strype, Ann. ibid. p. 144. See also Strype, Mem. π. 1, pp.
[front matter] 531, 532, and Zurich Letters, Parker Soc. ed. pp. 41, 111, 127, 205,
[front matter] &c. 2nd ed.

[front matter] And, above all, in the Convocation of the province of Canter-
[front matter] bury, held in 1586, among the “ Orders for the better increase
[front matter] of learning in the inferior Ministers,” introduced by Whitgift,
[front matter] Archbishop of Canterbury, the following direction stands fore-
[front matter] most :——“‘ Every minister having cure, and being under the
[front matter] degrees of master of arts, and batchelors of law, and not
[front matter] licensed to be a public preacher, shall before the second day
[front matter] of February next provide a Bible, and Bullinger’s Decads in
[front matter] Latin or English, and a paper book, and shall every day read
[front matter] over one chapter of the Holy Scriptures, and note the prin-
[front matter] cipal contentes thereof briefly in his paper booke, and shall
[front matter] every weeke read over one Sermon in the said Decads, and
[front matter] note likewise the chief matters therein contained in the said
[front matter] paper; and shall once in every quarter (viz. within a fort-
[front matter] night before or after the end of the quarter) shewe his said
[front matter] note to some preacher nere adjoyninge to be assigned for that
[front matter] purpose!.” And, agreebly with this order, it is recorded
[front matter] by Strype, Dr. Theophilus Aylmer, Archdeacon of London,
[front matter] acted in his visitation in the early part of the year 1587,—
[front matter] “the Bishop’s pious and painful son?.”
[front matter] Although a Memoir of Bullinger (together with indexes to
[front matter] the whole work) will be given in the last volume, it may be
[front matter] useful here to state briefly, that he was born at Bremgarten,
[front matter] near Zurich, on July 18, 1504; commenced his studies at
[front matter] the University of Cologne in 1519; began to unite himself to
[front matter] the divines of the Reformation in the course of 1524; was
[front matter] chosen pastor of Zurich, on the decease of C&colampadius, in
[front matter] the close of 1531; dedicated to Rodolph Gualter and others
[front matter] his first volume of the Decades, March 1, 1549; and died
[front matter] September 17, 1575, in the 71st year of his age®.
[front matter] N.B. The editing of these Decades having been com-
[front matter] menced by the Rev. Srevarr A. Pears, the notes which
[front matter] have the initial (P) affixed to them, are due to his research.

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.456] REGULATIONS FOR DELIVERY OF THE BOOKS PUBLISHED
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.456] BY THE SOCIETY.
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.456] They will be delivered, free of expense, at the office, or within three miles of the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.456] General Post Office, London.
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.456] II. They will be sent to any place in England beyond the distance of three miles from
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.456] the General Post Office, by any conveyance a member may point out. In this
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.456] case the parcels will be booked at the expense of the Society, but the carriage
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.456] must be paid by the members to whom they are sent.
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.456] III. They will be delivered, free of expense, at any place in London which a member
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.456] resident in the country may name.
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.456] IV. They may remain at the office of the Society until the members apply for them ;
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.456] but in that case, the Society will not be responsible for any damage which may
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.456] happen from fire, or other accident.
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.456] V. They will be sent to any of the Correspondents, or Agents of the Society, each
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.456] member paying the Correspondent or Agent a share of the carriage of the parcel
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.456] in which the books were included. Arrangements are made for the delivery on
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.456] this plan, in many of the cities and large towns where a sufficient number of
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.456] members reside; and it will be esteemed a favour if gentlemen who are willing to
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.456] further the objects of the Parker Society, by taking charge of the books for the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.456] members in their respective neighbourhoods, will write to the Office on the subject.
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.456] VI. ‘Chey will be delivered in Edinburgh and Dublin as in London, and forwarded
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.456] from thence to members in other parts of Scotland and Ireland, in the same
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.456] manner as is mentioned above with respect to England.

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.139] Now ceremonies are ordained either by God or men. As

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.143] Now, in reckoning up and touching these several cere-

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.143] monies do appertain to the ecclesiastical worship of God.
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.143] Therefore it is necessary that there should be persons appointed
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.143] in the church to be the masters, or rather public ministers, of
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.143] those ceremonies, to exercise and put them in practice, as the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.143] Lord ordained them. It is necessary also, that there be a
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.143] certain place and time appointed, wherein and when God
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.143] should be especially worshipped rather than at another place

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.143] monies, must be appointed and certainly numbered, that the

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.143] Levites; referring still the hearers to the reading of the holy
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.143] Bible, wherein the whole is fully contained and largely de-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.143] scribed.

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.183] [SERM.
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.183] bringing all the principles of our salvation and true godliness
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.183] into a brief summary, which, for the renewing and fulfilling
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.183] of all things, and for the abrogation of the old ceremonies,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.183] he called the new league, or new testament. In that testament
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.183] Christ alone is preached, the perfectness and fulness of all
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.183] things ; in it there is nothing more desired than faith and
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.183] charity; and in it is granted holy and wonderful liberty unto
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.183] the godly : of which I will speak at another time. But now
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.183] I return to the league which was renewed with Abraham.
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.183] We are expressly taught in Genesis, who they were that
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.183] made the league ; that is, the living, eternal, and omnipotent
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.183] God, who is the chief maker, preserver, and governor of all
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.183] things ; and Abraham with all his seed, that is, with all the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.183] faithful, of what nation or country soever they be. For so
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.183] doth the Apostle expound the seed of Abraham, especially in
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.183] his epistle to the Galatians, where he saith, " If ye be Christ's,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.183] then are ye the seed of Abraham, and heirs by promise."
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.183] The time, how long this league should endure, is eternal,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.183] and without end or term of time. For although, in the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.183] renewings or declarations of the league, many things were
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.183] added which afterward did vanish away, especially when
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.183] Christ was come in the flesh ; yet notwithstanding, in the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.183] substantial and chiefest points, ye can find nothing altered or
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.183] changed. For God is always the God of his people : he doth
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.183] always demand and require of them faithful obedience; as may
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.183] most evidently be perceived in the new Testament.
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.183] For there are two points, or especial conditions, contained

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] Divorcements and separations were permitted by the law
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] in the twenty-fourth of Deuteronomy, for nothing else but
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] for the hardness of the Jewish people's hearts, and for the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] avoiding of some greater inconvenience ; to wit, lest perad-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] venture any man should poison, strangle, or otherwise kill the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] woman, his wife, which he hated, when he could by none other
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] means rid his hands of her. And they that were in that
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] manner divorced might at their pleasures be married to
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] others.
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] Moreover, that justice might be maintained, and that
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] every man might enjoy his own, in the law there was charge
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] very diligently given for the division of things, for the parti-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] tion of the land of promise by equcil portions, and for the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] peculiar possession of proper goods ; that to every tribe pos-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] sessions might be given by lot, and that no man should by any
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] means make away the possessions which were given him. For
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] hereunto belongeth that which is spoken by Moses in the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] thirty-second, thirty-third, thirty-fourth chapters of the book
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] of Numbers, and oftentimes in other places also.
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] And yet notwithstanding, this law was nothing prejudicial
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] to traffic by exchange. For there were many and very upright
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] laws published for buying and selling, for letting and hiring,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] for borrowing and lending, for usury and things left in custody.
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] Whosoever desireth to see the places in the law, he shall have
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] them in the twenty-fifth of Leviticus, in the twenty-second of
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] Exodus, in the fifteenth and twenty-third chapters of Deute-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] ronomy. And I suppose that to this is to be referred the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] law which is given concerning pawns or pledges : " If thou
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] hast taken thy neighbour's garment to pledge, thou shalt
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] restore it him again before the sun be set. For that is his
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] only covering:" that is, it is the garment wherewith he
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] covereth his flesh, and wherein he sleepeth. "For it shall
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] come to pass, that if he cry to me, I will hear him ; because I
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] am merciful." Again; "Thou shalt not take the nether or
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] upper mill-stone to pledge : for he hath laid that whereon he
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.241] liveth to pledge to thee."

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.319] Now to this I will add such testimonies of scripture as
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.319] shall both better confirm and more plainly declare my ex-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.319] position. And, first of all, I will allege those testimonies

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.319] Zacharias the priest, and father of John Baptist, in his

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.319] freedom, I mean, wherein we, being by the Lord delivered
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.319] from all our enemies, both visible and invisible, should no
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.319] longer serve them with fear, but^ serve our God^ in joy and
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.319] gladness. There is added also the manner and order how
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.319] to serve him ; " in holiness and righteousness." Holiness
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.319] doth cut off and cast away all uncleanness and inconvenicncy^ :
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.319] righteousness giveth to every man that which is due, to wit,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.319] the things which we of duty do owe to every man, and doth
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.319] contain in it both freedom and benevolence. And in this
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.319] kind of service do they, which are made free, serve the Lord
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.319] their God, not for a day or two, or a certain few years, but
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.319] all the days of their life. Therefore true christian liberty
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.319] is the perpetual service which we owe and do to God.

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.329] Now we offend other men either by our words, or else
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.329] by our deeds. The offence that is given by words is partly
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.329] in evil, foolish, and unseasonable doctrine, and partly our
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.329] daily talk or communication. The greatest offence is that
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.329] which doth arise of wicked doctrine, directly contrary to the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.329] true doctrine of the holy gospel. The next to this is that
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.329] oft'ence which doth arise of foolish and unseasonable doctrine ;
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.329] which, though it be derived out of the word of God, is not-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.329] withstanding either unaptly uttered, or unwisely applied.
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.329] For the preacher may sin either by too much suffering^
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.329] or lenity ; or else by too much sharpness and overthwart
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.329] waywardness^, so that the hearers being offended do wholly
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.329] draw back from all hearing of the gospel. And yet, for
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.329] all this, the light of the gospel must not be hidden, nor the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.329] truth slily winked at^, because men will be offended ; but
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.329] preachers must with all their diligence take heed that the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.329] word of God be wisely set forth and aptly dispensed*. What-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.329] soever things are against the laws of God, those must most
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.329] constantly be accused, and without fear most dihgently con-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.329] futed, howsoever the world and worldlings do storm against
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.329] the same.
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.329] Now they do by their daily talk cause their brethren
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.329] to stumble, whosoever let their tongues run loose to talk
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.329] they care not what ; and at their pleasure, without advice,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.329] to babble they care not how : of which sort are filthy speech
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.329] and ribaldry, but especially such blasphemous words as are
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.329] unreverently uttered against God, the holy scriptures, and
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.329] articles of our faith ; for evil words corrupt good manners.
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.329] I do not here exclude the letters or writings of men which
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.329] do unadvisedly offend their brethren.

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.359] able to look into the faith of other men, which doth consist
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.359] in the mind ; and therefore we judge by their words and
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.359] deeds. Honest words and works bear witness of a faithful
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.359] heart ; whereas unhonest pranks and speeches do bewray a
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.359] kind of unbelief. The works of charity and humanity do
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.359] declare that we have faith in deed : whereas the lack of
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.359] them do argue the contrary. And therefore the scripture
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.359] admonisheth us, that the judgment shall be according to our
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.359] works. To this sense agreeth that in the twelfth of Matthew,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.359] where it is said, " By thy deeds^ thou shalt be justified, and
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.359] by the same thou shalt be condemned." To Abraham, after

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.359] only-begotten son, I will bless thee, and multiply thee ex-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.359] ceedingly, &c." But it is manifest that God made that
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.359] promise to Abraham before Isaac was born ; yea, he made
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.359] it as soon as Abraham was brought out of his country : there-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.359] fore the promise was not now first of all annexed as a reward
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.359] unto the works of Abraham, &c.
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.359] Therefore God examineth our works accordlns: to his
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.359] own favourable mercy, and not with the extremity and rigour

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.385] and is accomplished and finished by our own work and labour.

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.397] little, and laid it before your eyes, dearly beloved, for you

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.397] We are now come to demonstrate the first parts which
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.397] were set down in the description of sin immediately upon the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.397] beginning of this sermon. They are in number two : the first
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.397] is, "Sin is the natural corruption of mankind;" the latter
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.397] is, "And the action that riseth of it contrary to the law of
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.397] God." Some verily, in setting down the kinds or differences
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.397] of sins, do very well and advisedly say, "Of sins, one is
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.397] original, and another actual." I mean in order to speak of
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.397] both, so far as God shall give me grace : and first, of the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.397] same natural corruption in mankind ; that is, of original sin.
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.397] Now therefore it is called original sin, because it cometh
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.397] from the first beginning, being derived from our first parents
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.397] into us all by lineal descent and continual course from one to
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.397] another ; for we bring it with us in our nature from our
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.397] mother's womb into this life.
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.397] Of this sin there are many definitions made, which as
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.397] they do not disagree among themselves, so yet is one of them
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.397] more full and evident than another of them is. Some say,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.397] Original sin is the corruption of nature from the first perfect-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.397] ness. Other some say. It is the corruption of man's nature,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.397] which maketh that we do not truly obey the law of God, and
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.397] are not without sin. Again ; some call it a want, or defect ;
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.397] other call it concupiscence ; which might better seem to be the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.397] fruit of original sin, that is, of our corruption. Other call it
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.397] an inordinateness of appetites, which is left in nature^ An-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.397] selmus, a late writer, saith : " Original sin is the want of

[footnote decadesofbulling p.393] They object, that the scripture itself maketh mention of
[footnote decadesofbulling p.393] the death of the soul. I confess no less indeed. For the soul
[footnote decadesofbulling p.393] of man is both mortal and immortal, after a certain manner
[footnote decadesofbulling p.393] of his own. For the soul is not all manner of ways immortal
[footnote decadesofbulling p.393] as God is, of whom it is said that he only hath immortality.
[footnote decadesofbulling p.393] And truly the death of the soul in the holy scripture is to be
[footnote decadesofbulling p.393] remembered; but the same is referred to the state and con-
[footnote decadesofbulling p.393] dition, not to the substance, of the soul. For if God be the
[footnote decadesofbulling p.393] life of the soul, surely to be forsaken of God, and to be left
[footnote decadesofbulling p.393] unto thyself, is the death of the soul. But nevertheless the
[footnote decadesofbulling p.393] reasonable soul liveth in his proper essence or being, so that,
[footnote decadesofbulling p.393] when it liveth miserably, a miserable life is in very deed
[footnote decadesofbulling p.393] called death. But desperation also is the very death of the
[footnote decadesofbulling p.393] soul; for by hope we live: and Paul saith, “I live, yet
[footnote decadesofbulling p.393] not I, but Christ liveth in me; and the life which I now live
[footnote decadesofbulling p.393] in the flesh, I live by the faith of the Son of God.” Therefore
[footnote decadesofbulling p.393] they that are destitute of faith are dead, and they that have
[footnote decadesofbulling p.393] faith live. St Augustine, cap. 10, De Fide et Symbolo, saith:

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.49] all their works openly that they may be seen of men, firmly
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.49] trusting and stiffly standing to men's traditions. To these it
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.49] is a custom and property not only to fly from the church which
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.49] teacheth the righteousness of Christ, but also to curse, detest,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.49] and to persecute it with all cruelty. Such kind of people
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.49] were the Jews and Jewish Pharisees, with whom our Lord
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.49] Jesus Christ had much contention, and with whom even at
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.49] this day the church contcndeth and maketh wars. These be
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.49] the plain and visible members of the devil's church, and they
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.49] are not to be counted of the outward2 church, yea, they are
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.49] not once worthy to be named in the church of Christ. Again,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.49] there are some kind of hypocrites that are dissemblers, which
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.49] neither give any confidence to their own righteousness and
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.49] justice, neither yet do greatly regard the traditions of men.
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.49] These kinds of people neither hate the church, nor fly from it,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.49] nor persecute it; but outwardly they agree with it, professing the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.49] same faith, and participating the selfsame sacraments : but in-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.49] wardly and in mind they neither believe unfeignedly and sin-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.49] cerely, neither do they live holily. Of this sort, some of them
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.49] for a season will cleave to the fellowship and company of the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.49] church ; and having any occasion given they will fall from it,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.49] as heretics and schismatics are wont to do, and such as of
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.49] friends are become enemies. Other there be again that never
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.49] fall from the church, but keep themselves in the fellowship of
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.49] the church all their lifetime, outwardly pretending and feign-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.49] ing religion ; but inwardly giving themselves up to their own

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.224] those that be set in authority, " that we may lead a quiet and
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.224] peaceable life in all godliness and honesty." Private persons are
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.224] our parents, wife, children, kinsfolk, allies, neighbours, citizens,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.224] friends, enemies, sick persons, captives, such as are afflicted,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.224] and, to be short, all that are nigh about us, whose health and
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.224] safety nature and Christian charity willeth by prayers to
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.224] commend unto God; and whereof there are also testimonies and
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.224] examples in the scripture. But the things we should pray
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.224] for are those good things that are to be desired ; whereof
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.224] some are heavenly, spiritual, or eternal ; and other earthly,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.224] corporal, or temporal. Moreover, some things verily are com-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.224] mon, other some again are private : those things that are
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.224] common pertain to the whole church and commonwealth ;
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.224] neither belong they to a few, as do private things. And
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.224] spiritual things are chiefly reckoned to be these; faith, hope,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.224] charity, perseverance, and that whole company of all manner
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.224] virtues, the profit and safety of the church, forgiveness of
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.224] sins, and life everlasting. Among the which not unfitly are
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.224] reckoned the gifts of understanding, the liberal sciences, well

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] ordered schools, faithful teachers, godly magistrates, and up-

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] strong and valiant armies for war, health, strength, and come-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] liness of body, abundance or sufficient wealth, the safe pros-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] perity of wife and children, the protection and defence of
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] friends and citizens, peace, a good name, and other things
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] which are of this kind. But no man is ignorant, that we
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] ought to have a greater care of spiritual things than corporal
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] things, and principally to desire heavenly things. And in
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] corporal things there is also a choice to be used ; that the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] profit of the commonwealth be preferred before our own
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] private gain. For the commonwealth continuing in safety,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] the citizens may also be safe ; and so long as schools and
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] universities, or places of learning, be maintained, there is
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] hope that the commonwealth shall never be destitute of
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] wise and upright governors. There are also in temporal
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] goods some better than other some : those things that are
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] best, therefore, the saints or godly men do chiefly require of
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] the Lord ; and nevertheless those which are of less value they
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] understand to come from him, and therefore they ask them
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] also of the Lord. They that are but meanly exercised in
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] the scriptures affirm, that it is not lawful in prayer to ask
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] corporal goods of the Lord ; but they are confuted by many
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] examples of the scripture. For not only the patriarchs and
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] prophets, but also the apostles of Christ, asked temporal goods
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] of the Lord; as defence against their enemies, a good report,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] and other things necessary for the body. Which thing we
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] shall learn anon by the form of prayer which the Lord him-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] self hath taught us, diligently shewing us what we should ask.
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] This also cometh in question, In what tongue prayer
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] must be made ? They that affirm that privately and publicly
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] we must pray in Latin, seem in my judgment to be out of
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] their wits, unless they speak of such as are skilful in the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] Latin tongue. For since we must pray, not only with mouth
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] and voice, but also with heart and mind ; how, I pray you,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] shall he pray with heart and mind, who useth a language
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] he understandeth not ? Indeed, he uttereth godly words, but
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] he knoweth not what he saith. For it cometh all to one
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] reckoning, to pray never a whit or not at all, and to babble
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.225] out words which are not understood. Let every nation there-

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] for word that most holy form of praying, orderly made with
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] most divine words even by the mouth of the Lord, as Mat-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] thew the apostle hath left it recorded unto us ; and then to
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] expound the same as briefly and plainly as may be, to the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] intent that every one may the better understand what he
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] prayeth, and feel a more effectual working inwardly. Of that
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] most heavenly prayer this is the form :
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] O our Father, which art in heaven ; hallowed be thy
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done, as well
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] in earth, as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] bread. And forgive us our trespasses*, as we forgive
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] them that trespass against us|. And lead us not into
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] temptation, but deliver us from evil. Amen.
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] This most holy prayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, our
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] saviour, our doctor or teacher, and highest priest, delivered to
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] the catholic church to be a catholic form or rule to pray unto
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] God, is wont to be divided into a little preface, and six
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] petitions. Some reckon seven. Some say, that the three former
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] petitions serve chiefly to the spreading abroad of God's glory ;
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] the three latter concern the care of ourselves, and ask those
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] things that are needful for us. But they seem in manner
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] all1 to contain both.
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] The little preface is this : " 0 our Father, which art in
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] heaven." By this we call upon God ; and, dedicating ourselves
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] unto him, we commit ourselves wholly unto his protection and
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] mercy. And every word hath his high mysteries ; for our
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] Lord would have us rather pray with understanding than
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] with words. These therefore do admonish us, and suffice to
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] be thought upon. But the mind, being instructed with the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] Holy Ghost, which I told you is needful before all things to
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] them that pray, and being lifted up to the beholding of God
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] and of heavenly things, doth devoutly and ardently meditate
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] these things.
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] And truly the word, " Father," putteth us in mind of
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] many things together. For first, it teacheth us, that all our
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] prayers ought to be 2 offered to none other than to him, which
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] is a father ; that is to say, that only God is to be called upon,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] and not another for him, or another with him. For our God
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.243] and Father is one, the fulness and sufficiency of all good things,

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.255] man is said to be blessed, which suffereth temptation : " for
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.255] when he is tried, he shall receive the crown of life." We
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.255] pray also1, that we be not led into temptation: for the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.255] devil likewise tempteth ; we are tempted of the world, and of
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.255] our flesh. There are temptations on our right hand and on
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.255] our left ; tending to this end, to overthrow us, to drown us in
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.255] the bottomless pit of our sins, and thereby to destroy us:
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.255] when that is done, we are not only tempted, but we are led
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.255] into and also entrapped in temptation. Such a petition there-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.255] fore we do make : If it please thee, 0 heavenly Father, to
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.255] exercise us with thy wholesome temptations, we beseech thee
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.255] grant that we may be found tried2: and suffer us not to be
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.255] led by a devilish and wicked temptation ; that, leaving thee,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.255] and being made bond-slaves to our enemy, and drowned in
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.255] the gulf of wickednesses, we be caught and kept of him in evil,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.255] sin, and in our own destruction. For now we add the con-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.255] trary clause, which also expoundeth the former ; which, as
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.255] other say, is the seventh petition : "But deliver us from evil ;"
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.255] ctwo tou irovripov ; I say, from that evil, to wit, from Satan,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.255] who elsewhere is called a tempter. Deliver us from Satan,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.255] and from all evils which he sendeth : deliver us from snares,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.255] crafty practices, deceivings ; from war, famine, captivity,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.255] plague ; from all those things which are evil, hurtful, and
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.255] dangerous. Those things that are such our heavenly Father
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.255] knoweth very well, to whom we say here : " Give us healthful
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.255] and good things ; take away from us those things which
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.255] thou knowest to be hurtful and evil."

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.255] moreover, " Amen." That confirmation and giving of assent

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.255] see in Deut. xxvii., Nehem. viii., 1 Cor. xiv. The same in
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.255] the beginning 3 doth express our desire ; for we confess that
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.255] we desire those things heartily which we pray for. Besides
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.255] that, it declareth the certainty of our faith ; as if we should

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.269] whereby Christ is declared to be Lord of all, Lord of life and

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.269] Exod. i\\, are called in the scripture signs ; for they were
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.269] witnesses both of God's lawful sending, and tokens of his
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.269] mighty power to be executed against Egypt : but neither had
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.269] these any ceremony, neither gathered together into any society.

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.269] his preaching he prophesied should fall upon them4. The
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.269] like we may see in Ezech. the xviith. and xxivth. chap. These
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.269] signs paradigmatical, or for example, are in some things like

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.269] they are certain mixed chrice, so termed, for that they consist

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.269] active chria, " to be that which declareth and plainly shew-

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.321] [SERM.
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.321] fathers moved no strife nor contentions about the sacraments,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.321] as are at this day among us. For as they did beautify
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.321] the signs with the names of the things (signified), so did they
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.321] acknowledge the kind of speech ; neither did they roughly
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.321] urge the words, as though the very signs were really and
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.321] corporally that selfsame thing which they signified. There-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.321] fore this canon or rule is so often repeated and beaten upon
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.321] by Aurelius Augustine, "That the signs do take or borrow the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.321] names of things signified1." By the same canon or rule he
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.321] maketh plain certain dark places ; of which thing we will now
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.321] set down some testimonies. In hialZpist. 23. ad Bonifaciina,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.321] de Parvulorum Baptismate, he saith : " If sacraments had not
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.321] some likeness with those things whereof they are sacraments,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.321] no doubt they were no sacraments ; for of this likeness, for the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.321] most part, they take the names of the things themselves. As
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.321] also the apostle, speaking of baptism, saith, « We are buried
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.321] with Christ by baptism into his death.' He doth not say,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.321] we signify the burial; but he doth flatly say, 'we are buried.'
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.321] Therefore he called the sacrament of so great a thing no
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.321] otherwise but by the name of the selfsame thing2." And in
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.321] Tract, super Joan. 63: " When the unclean person is gone,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.321] all which remain are clean. Such a like thing shall there
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.321] be, when the world, being overcome of Christ, shall pass
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.321] away, and there shall no unclean person remain among the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.321] people of God ; when, the tares being separated from the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.321] wheat, the just shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.321] Father. The Lord foreseeing this would come to pass, and
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.321] now witnessing that it was signified, when Judas fell away as
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.321] tares separated, the holy apostles remaining as wheat, he saith,

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] [SERM.
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] For there are many peculiar things done in the scripture, out
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] of which if any man shall go about to draw general things
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] and common laws, he shall bring in absurdities innumerable.
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] What if Moses in the same place doth only describe the deed
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] of his wife, moved thereunto by anger and displeasure, and not
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] for religion's sake, to perform the ministry unto God? For
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] she, grudging1 against her husband, yea, and against God,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] took the foreskin of her son which was cut away, and cast it
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] at his father her husband's feet, not without reproach, saying :
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] "A bloody husband art thou unto me." As if you should say :
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] Ich habb woll ein bluotigman an dirr2. And though the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] angel was appeased with Moses, because he seemed to allow
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] the deed of the woman as well pleasing God ; yet that is more
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] to be imputed to the mercy of God, rather than to the righte-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] ousness of the woman's deed. It did grievously displease God,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] that David had slain Urias, and moreover had taken Beerseba
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] to himself to wife ; yet of his goodness and singular mercy he
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] vouchsafed to call Salomon, who was born of Beersabe, by this
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] name, Jedidia, because the Lord loved him. So the gracious
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] Lord is also reconciled with Moses, who either by his own negli-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] gence, or through the fault of his Madianitish wife, lingered
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] circumcision in the body of her son against the law longer
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] than was meet ; and is content with, and taketh in good part, the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] circumcision, which the woman performed rather of indignation
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] than for religion : yet he will not that after her, as a perfect
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] example, other women should circumcise.
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] But, you say, by baptism ministered by a woman the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] peril of death or eternal damnation was to be prevented, into
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] which the infant falleth if he depart this world without bap-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] tism. My answer is : When the infant, being newly delivered
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] out of his mother's womb, departeth with too too speedy death,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] so that the parents cannot, though they would never so fain,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] bring him to be baptized of the minister of the church, this
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] pinch of necessity truly is not to the damnation or death of the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] infant ; because he, being received into the covenant by the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] grace of God, is delivered from death through the blood of the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] Son of God. We are not destitute of testimonies of scripture
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] duly serving in this behalf. In the law it was not lawful
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.409] t1 impotenter obstrepens, Lat.]

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] First we say, that the supper of the Lord is an action or
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] deed. For the Lord, when he made his supper, did give
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] thanks unto God ; he brake bread and gave the cup, and said,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] " Do this in the remembrance of me." Again, it cannot be
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] every action. For at the table, where we eat meat, we also
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] give thanks unto God, we break bread and give the cup :
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] but it is an holy action, because it is from God and instituted
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] unto the church. Wherefore it far differeth from our ordi-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] nary meat-suppers ; as well for that it is specially instituted
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] by the Son of God unto the church, as also because it hath
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] the word of God and the peculiar example of Christ. There-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] fore St Paul, making a difference between this and common
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] eating, saith : " If any man hunger, let him eat at home; lest
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] that ye come together to your condemnation.1' And again :
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] " Have ye not houses to eat and drink in ?" As though he
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] might say, This supper is mystical. Again, what manner of
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] action it is, it doth forthwith appear by that which followeth;
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] where the Lord, by the setting of bread and wine before us
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] at the banquet, doth assure us of his promise and communion,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] &c. This supper therefore hath his peculiar limits ; of the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] which although I spake when I entreated generally of the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] virtue of the sacraments, yet will I repeat certain of them
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] that make most for this purpose, when I shall draw toward
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] an end of this sermon.
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] But concerning the description1 of this supper, these things
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] are chiefly to be considered and declared. First, who did
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] institute it, and who is the true author and maker2 of the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] Lord's supper. Not any man, but the very Son of God himself,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] the wisdom of the Father, very God and man : so that we
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] come not to the table of men, although a man being the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] minister be the chiefest there ; neither do we receive holy
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] signs at the hands of the minister only, but also at the hand
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] of our Lord himself3, whose guests we are if we be faithful.
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] He hath consecrated the supper for us, and doth yet con-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] secrate it by his holy word, his will, and his power : of
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] which matter we spake before. And because the faithful
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.441] understand and know these things, they sit down to the holy

[running head] THE FIFTH DECADE.
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] [SERM.
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] The matter is indifferent, whether the church take the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] supper sitting down, or going to the table ; whether a man
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] take the holy mysteries in his own hand, or receive it into his
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] mouth at the hands of him that ministereth. It is most a^ree-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] able with the first simplicity and institution of the supper, to
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] sit, and to receive the sacraments in a man's own hands of him
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] that ministereth ; and afterwards to break it, eat it, and to di-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] vide it unto others. For as the Lord sat at table with his
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] disciples, so he reached forth the mysteries, saying : " Take,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] and divide it among you." Moreover, as there is more quiet-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] ness and less stir in sitting at the supper, while the ministers
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] carry the holy mysteries about the congregation ; so it is well
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] known by histories of antiquity, that the sacrament hath
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] been delivered into the hands of the communicants. It is mere
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] superstition and repugnant to the doctrine of the apostles, to
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] scrape the hands of the lay people that have touched the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] holy sacrament of the supper. Why do they not also by
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] the same law scrape the lips, tongue, and jaws of the com-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] municants ?
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] Of these things before handled springeth another ques-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] tion : What is to be thought of the remnants and leavings of
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] the Lord's supper ; and whether there ought any part of it to
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] be reserved ; and whether that which is reserved or shut up
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] ought to be adored ? This question seemeth to have no godli-
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] ness at all in it, but to be altogether superstitious and very
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] hurtful. For who knoweth not, that bread and wine, out of the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] holy and lawful use appointed, are not a sacrament? Shall
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] we proceed to demand with these sophisters, what that is
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] which the mouse gnaweth when he gnaweth the Lord's bread ?
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] These questions are most unworthy to be demanded, and to
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] be raked up in holy oblivion. Touching the shutting up of
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] the sacrament, the Lord teacheth us not one word in the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] gospel, much less of worshipping it. " Take," saith he, " eat,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] and divide it among you." He saith not, Lay it up, and
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] worship it ; for the true worshippers worship the Father in
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] spirit and truth. Moreover, we read how the Lord hath
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] plainly said in the gospel : " If they say unto you, Behold,
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] where he is in the desert, go not forth ; behold, where he is in
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] the innermost parts of the house, do not believe." He setteth
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] down the cause of this his commandment : " For like as the
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.459] lightning goeth forth of the east, and appeareth in the west,
[margin decadesofhenrybu p.460] coi.ui. what  time  to

[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.531] place4. Moreover, it is fit that due portions be paid to
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.531] priests, schoolmasters, scholars5, and to all other ecclesiastical
[footnote decadesofhenrybu p.531] persons whatsoever.

[index] THE
[index] ELEVENTH ANNUAL REPORT
[index] (FOR THE YEAR 1851.)
[index] OF
[index] Stye \laxKcx Soctetjj,
[index] INSTITUTED A.D. 1840.
[index] FOR THE PUBLICATION OF
[index] THE WORKS OF THE FATHERS AND EARLY WRITERS OF THE
[index] REFORMED ENGLISH CHURCH.
[index] PRESENTED TO THE GENERAL MEETING, MAY THE 25th, 1851.
[index] " He (Archbishop Parker) was a great collector of ancient and modern writings, and took es
[index] care of the safe preservation of them for all succeeding times; as foreseeing, undoubtedly
[index] might be made of them by posterity ; that, by having recourse to such originals and preced
[index] knowledge of things might the batter appear."
[index] " As he was a great patron and promoter of good learning, so he took care of giving encour
[index] toprinting— a great instrument of the increase thereof."
[index] Strype's Life of Archbishop Parker.
[index] The Council of the Parker Society at the close of their eleventh year have to
[index] lay before the Members the following Report : —
[index] Four books have been completed and circulated for 1851. These are —
[index] A third Volume of Bullinger's Decades,
[index] Private Prayers, put forth by authority during the reign of Queen Elizabeth,
[index] A first portion of Archbishop Whitgift's Writings, and
[index] Bishop Woolton's Christian Manual.
[index] Little need be said in commendation of such books as these. The Council
[index] may, however, remind Subscribers that in the works of Archbishop Whitgift an
[index] entirely new field is opened out. Hitherto the controversial treatises they have
[index] published, as of Ridley, Cranmer, Jewel, and others, have been directed against
[index] the Romanists, and almost every point of dispute which could arise with them
[index] has been fully discussed and elucidated ; so that those who are called to con-
[index] tend against the corruptions of the Papacy may find efficient weapons in the
[index] armories of the men who hi this country led the van-guard of the Reformation.
[index] 2 THE ELEVENTH REPORT OF THE COUNCIL.
[index] But, after the Church had been purified in the reign of Elizabeth, there
[index] arose domestic dissension. There were men who were dissatisfied with the
[index] decent forms which had been retained: and their dissatisfaction grew, till almost
[index] every part of the polity of the Church was censured and attacked. It was
[index] Whitgift's purpose to repel these attacks, and to prove thai there was no order
[index] of the Church of England winch did not find a warrant in Scripture and
[index] Christian antiquity. His great work " The Defence of the Answer to the
[index] Admonition," must always be regarded as one of the most important pro-
[index] ductions of the age. It is a portion of this which has now been published.
[index] The Council have issued another volume of their smaller series, Bishop
[index] Woolton's "Christian Manual," which will, they think, be acceptable to the
[index] Members. In this series it has been " designed " (to quote the words of the
[index] advertisement prefixed to Woolton) " to exhibit the spirit and principles of the
[index] Reformation in their various forms of development, as they influenced the
[index] literature and character of the age. The first of these publications was an
[index] illustration of its devotional character; the second, of the poetical, as poetry
[index] lent its aid in furtherance of the great struggle for spiritual and intellectual
[index] emancipation ; the third of the directly spiritual and experimental working
[index] of religion ; the fourth, of its controversial phase on a smaller scale ; and the
[index] fifth and last, of the application of its principles to the practical duties of
[index] individual and social life. In all these different aspects they present a com-
[index] bined testimony to the power and value of the blessed Reformation."
[index] In reference to future proceedings, the Council have to announce that two
[index] more volumes of Whitgift are in preparation, also the concluding volumes
[index] respectively of Bullinger, Bradford, and Bishop Hooper, with Rogers on the
[index] Articles, the Correspondence of Archbishop Parker, and Nowell's Catechisms.
[index] These works they hope to issue in the years 1852 and 1853, when the proceed-
[index] ings of the Society will close. But, as some of these volumes must be bidky,
[index] it is necessary to say that they cannot all be published unless the present
[index] number of subscribers shall be fully kept up. It is earnestly hoped, therefore,
[index] that the Members will continue their subscriptions for the brief remaining period
[index] of the Society's existence, and thus enable the Council satisfactorily to bring
[index] their labours to an end. They would feel it a real misfortune, if they should
[index] be obliged to omit any of the works just named from their list.
[index] In contemplating what has been done, the Council have abundant cause
[index] for gratitude to God. The support afforded them has far outrun their original
[index] anticipations, and they are convinced that the writings they have heen the means
[index] of putting forth have indeed the strongest claims on the attention of Christian
[index] men. They are the writings of those whose memory deserves to be cherished
[index] with sentiments of profound and grateful veneration. They are the writings
[index] of those to whom under God we owe the privileges we at present enjoy. The
[index] works of such men woidd in any circumstances be important: they are more
[index] especially so, as the Council have before reminded the Subscribers, because
[index] they assume, in a measure, the authentic character of documents, and have
[index] thus an especial bearing and weighty influence upon almost every theological
[index] question which can agitate the Church. Heretofore they were in the reach
[index] of comparatively few individuals, and some of them were all but inaccessible:
[index] it has been the work of the Parker Society to circulate them so extensively
[index] that they can never again be overlooked, and to place them by their cheapness
[index] within the reach of students in general.

[index] TIIE LAWS OF THE PARKER SOCIETY.
[index] LAWS OF THE PARKER SOCIETY
[index] I. — That the Society shall be called The Parker Society, and that its
[index] objects shall be — first, the reprinting, without abridgement, alteration, or
[index] omission, of the best Works of the Fathers and Early "Writers of the Reformed
[index] English Church, published in the period between the accession of King Edward
[index] VI. and the death of Queen Elizabeth ; secondly, the printing of such remains
[index] of other Writers of the Sixteenth Century as may appear desirable (including
[index] under both Classes, some of the early English Translations of the Foreign
[index] Reformers ; ) and thirdly, the printing of some manuscripts of the same Authors,
[index] hitherto unpublished.
[index] II. — That the Society shall consist of such a number of members, being
[index] subscribers of, at least, One Pound each annually, as the Council may determine -T
[index] the subscription to be considered due on the First clay of January in each year,
[index] in advance, and to be paid on or before such a day as the Council may fix ;
[index] sufficient notice being given of the day appointed.
[index] III. — That the Management of the Society shall be vested in a President,,
[index] a Treasurer, a Librarian, and a Council of twenty four other subscribers,,
[index] being Members of the Established Church, of whom not less than sixteen
[index] shall be Clergymen. The Council and Officers to be elected annually by the
[index] subscribers, at a General Meeting to be held in the month of May, or
[index] immediately after ; and no persons shall then be proposed who are not already
[index] members of the Council, or Officers, unless their names shall have been trans-
[index] mitted to the Secretaries on or before the 15th of April in the current year,
[index] by nominations in writing, signed by at least five subscribers. And that
[index] there be three Secretaries appointed by the Council ; also that the Council
[index] have power to fill all vacancies during the year.
[index] IV. — That the accounts of the receipt and expenditure of the Society shall
[index] be examined every year, previously to the General Meeting, by four Auditors,
[index] two of them selected from the Council, and two appointed by the preceding
[index] General Meeting.
[index] V. — That the fimds shall be expended in the payment of the expense
[index] incurred in producing the works published by the Society, so that every mem-
[index] ber not in arrear of his or her annual subscription shall receive a copy of every
[index] work published by the Society during the year, for each sum of One Pound
[index] subscribed, without any charge for the same ; and that the number of copies-
[index] printed in each year shall be limited to the quantity required for the number
[index] actually subscribed for.
[index] VI.— That every member of the Society who shall intimate to the Council
[index] a desire to withdraw, or who shall not pay the subscription by the time ap-
[index] pointed, shall cease to be a member of the Society ; and no member shall at
[index] any time incur any liability beyond the annual subscription.
[index] VII. — That, after the commencement of the procedings, no rule shall be
[index] made or altered excepting at a General Meeting and after notice of the same
[index] lias been communicated to the members by circulars, or by advertisement in
[index] two London daily newspapers, at least fourteen days before the General
[index] Meeting.
[index] VIII. — Donations and Legacies will be thankfully received ; the amount
[index] of which shall be expended by the Council in supplying copies of the publi-
[index] cations to clerical, or other libraries, destitute of funds to purchase the same,
[index] and for such other purposes, connected with the objects of the Society, as the
[index] Council may determine.

[index] REGULATIONS FOR DELIVERY OF THE BOOKS PUBLISHED
[index] BY THE SOCIETY.
[index] I. They will be delivered, free of expense, at the office, or within three miles of the
[index] General Post Office, London.
[index] II. They will be sent to any place in England beyond the distance of three miles from
[index] the General Post Office, by any conveyance a member may point out. In this
[index] case the parcels will be booked at the expense of the Society, but the carriage
[index] must be paid by the members to whom they are sent.
[index] III. They will be delivered, free of expense, at any place in London which a member
[index] resident in the country7 may name.
[index] IV. They may remain at the office of the Society, until the members apply for them ;
[index] but, in that case, the Society will not be responsible for any damage which may
[index] happen from fire, or other accident.
[index] V. They will be sent to any of the Correspondents, or Agents of the Society, each
[index] member paying the Correspondent or Agent a share of the carriage of the" parcel
[index] in which the books were included. Arrangements are made for the delivery on
[index] this plan, in many of the cities and large towns where a sufficient number of
[index] members reside; and it will be esteemed a favour if gentlemen who are willing to
[index] further the objects of the Parker Society, by taking charge of the books for the
[index] members in their respective neighbourhoods, will write to the Office on the subject.
[index] VI. They will be delivered in Edinburgh and Dublin as in London, and forwarded
[index] from thence to members in other parts of Scotland and Ireland, in the same
[index] manner as is mentioned above with respect to England.
